                                     I.        Introduction and Summary
        Continuing the extraordinary nature of this proceeding, 134 parties (including the M31,
M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners (Party No. 631)) filed initial briefs in this case. Often en-
tire CCN proceedings are resolved—from application to final order—in less than 134 total filings.1
After reading those briefs, the M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners timely file this reply.2
        The M31, M32, and M33 Opposition Landowners’ initial brief (1) emphasized their oppo-
sition to Links M31, M32, and M33; (2) compared the eight “Routes of Interest” across all the
statutory and regulatory routing factors; and (3) concluded that Route 894 is the best alternative
proposed transmission-line route (with Routes 487 and 891 also being acceptable alternatives,
which might have a less negative effect on certain landowners). 3 The M31, M32, and M33 Oppo-
sition Landowners also explained that the Texas Parks and Wildlife Department (“TPWD”) neither
provided recommendations or informational comments to the Commission regarding the Project
nor intervened in this proceeding. 4

the parties supporting Routes 572 5 and Cherokee G (“CCG”). 6 Routes 572 and CCG are two south-

        Only six parties recommend Route 572 10 or Route CCG. 11 And those parties’ recommen-
dations are not persuasive. Three parties’ support for Route 572 or Route CCG can be dispatched
at the outset. Then, for the remaining three parties, this brief rebuts three specific arguments that
those parties advance to distract from the flaws of Routes 572 and CCG.

  A.          Three intervenors supporting Route 572 or Route CCG fail to sufficiently explain
                      why those routes should be selected over Route 894 or Route 487.

         1.         Carpenter Land and Cattle Co. provides no explanation for its cursory
                    support for Route 572.

the ALJs and the Commission to follow the links in Route 296 or Route 572.” 12 Other than that
one reference to Route 572, Carpenter doesn’t discuss Route 572 at all. The rest of Carpenter’s
brief exclusively supports Route 296 with no argument supporting Route 572. 13
        What Carpenter does explain is that it opposes Route 894 because that route includes
Link J22, which impacts Carpenter’s land. 14 So conversely, Carpenter supports Route 296 because
it doesn’t include Link J22 or impact Carpenter’s land. 15 But Carpenter fails to explain why it

        1.         Routes 572 and CCG are materially longer, costlier, and more harmful to
                   habitable structures than Route 894 or Route 487.
         Although routing isn’t simply “a mathematical exercise,” 47 it also cannot be solely left up
to “agency-expertise vibes.” 48 Length, cost, and habitable-structure count provide real, hard num-
bers for the ALJs and the Commission to evaluate in each CCN proceeding when determining a
transmission line’s impact to ratepayers’ wallets and Texans’ land, homes, churches, schools, and
businesses. Routes 487 and 894 appropriately minimize those impacts. And reviewing quantitative
data in no way “reduce[s] the analysis to a numerical exercise that gives a feeling of objectivity.”49
Quite the opposite. Reviewing and comparing quantitative routing data is the only way for the
ALJs and the Commission to accurately consider and balance the routing factors while “find[ing]
a resolution that is least harmful on the community and the property owners involved.” 50
         First, costs. Route 572 costs almost $25 million more than Route 487 and over $8 million
more than Route 894. 51 Even worse, Route CCG costs $90 million more than Route 487 and $74
million more than Route 894. 52 The few proponents of Routes 572 and CCG either downplay those
large cost increases as “amounting to only minor variations in the total project budget” 53 that can
be “absorb[ed]” by ratepayers 54 or ignore them altogether. 55 The ALJs and the Commission should
not follow their lead. As Commission Staff witness John Poole explained, the range of costs in this
case “would be the cost of the entire transmission line in other cases . . . [t]hat’s a pretty significant
cost.” 56 Mr. Poole agreed that even though the percentage differences might be “deemed to be
